summary: Describes how an OSPF router can advertise its local addresses in OSPF Traffic Engineering extensions. Other routers need these addresses to compute traffic-engineered MPLS paths to a router's addresses, but previously only addresses tied to TE links were advertised. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Routers announce more of their own street addresses to neighbors, so others can plan a route that ends right at their door.

questions: advertise router local addresses in ospf te
how to compute te lsp to a router address
what is the ospf node attribute tlv
how to advertise loopback addresses in ospf te
subtitle: How an OSPF router tells its neighbors about loopback and other local addresses so traffic-engineered paths can end there.

tldr.problem: OSPF TE extensions advertise only a router's ID and the addresses of its TE-enabled links, so other routers cannot compute MPLS TE paths to its loopback or non-TE interface addresses.
tldr.mechanism: A new Node Attribute TLV (type 5) in the TE LSA carries a Node IPv4 Local Address sub-TLV (type 1) and a Node IPv6 Local Address sub-TLV (type 2) listing the extra addresses.
tldr.outcome: Routers can fill their traffic engineering database with these addresses and compute CSPF paths to them. The RFC updates RFC 3630 and is itself updated by RFC 6827 and RFC 8687.

today: RFC 5786 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3630. It has been updated by RFC 6827 and RFC 8687, and it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Local Addresses Are Missing
sections.content:
Sometimes an operator wants a constrained shortest path first (CSPF) computed MPLS TE LSP to a router address that is not in the TE LSAs, such as a loopback or a non-TE interface address. One example in the RFC is a network carrying VPN and non-VPN traffic: one loopback address may be the BGP next-hop for VPN traffic and another the next-hop for non-VPN traffic, so two separate TE LSPs, one to each loopback, are desirable.

The catch is that the OSPF TE extensions of RFC 3630 and RFC 5329 advertise only the router ID and the local addresses of TE-enabled links. Other routers can put those into their traffic engineering database (TED), but not the rest.

Existing OSPF data does not fill the gap. OSPFv2 stub links in the router LSA (RFC 2328) do not reveal all local addresses: for a subnetted point-to-point interface the stub link ID is the subnet address, and for a non-subnetted one it is the neighbor address. OSPFv3 intra-prefix LSAs (RFC 5340) are also not sufficient.
sections.eli5: Imagine a house with several doors, but the neighbors were only ever told about two of them. If you want to deliver a package to a different door, nobody knows it exists.

sections.title: The Rejected Alternative and the Chosen Approach
sections.content:
One idea was to advertise a TE link TLV for each local address, possibly with a new link type. The RFC rejects it as inefficient, because the only meaningful information is the address. It would also force implementations to treat these TE link TLVs differently from others: the TE metric is normally a mandatory sub-TLV but would mean nothing for a local address.

The chosen solution is to advertise the local addresses in a new Node Attribute TLV inside the OSPF TE LSA. The RFC anticipates that this TLV will prove more generally useful than this one purpose.
sections.eli5: Instead of pretending each extra address is a whole road, they made a simple new notice board just for a router's own addresses.

sections.title: The Node Attribute TLV and Its Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The Node Attribute TLV carries attributes of a router. Its type is 5, its length is variable, and it holds one or more sub-TLVs. This RFC defines two.

The Node IPv4 Local Address sub-TLV has type 1. Each address is a <Prefix Length, Prefix> tuple: the prefix length takes 1 byte (at most 32) and the prefix takes 4 bytes, with zero bits as necessary. The sub-TLV length, in octets, is the sum of the lengths of all the encodings.

The Node IPv6 Local Address sub-TLV has type 2. Each address MUST be encoded as in RFC 5340 with three fields: PrefixLength (8 bits), PrefixOptions (8 bits) and Address Prefix. The address prefix is padded with zero bits to a multiple of 32-bit words and consumes (PrefixLength + 31) / 32 such words.
sections.eli5: Each address is written on a small label with its length and its number. One label type is for the older kind of address and another for the newer, longer kind.

sections.title: What a Router Advertises
sections.content:
A router announces one or more local addresses in the Node Attribute TLV. Addresses that can already be learned from TE LSAs, namely the router address and TE interface addresses, SHOULD NOT be repeated in the node local address sub-TLV. What is advertised depends on the router's local configuration, and the default behavior MAY be to advertise all loopback interface addresses.

There are strict limits on repetition. The Node Attribute TLV MUST NOT appear in more than one TE LSA originated by a router, and such an LSA MUST NOT include more than one Node Attribute TLV. A Node Attribute TLV MUST NOT carry more than one Node IPv4 Local Address sub-TLV, nor more than one Node IPv6 Local Address sub-TLV.
sections.eli5: A router lists only the extra addresses nobody knew about, usually its loopbacks, and it does so in one single notice, not many.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it does not introduce any further security issues beyond those discussed in RFC 3630 and RFC 5329. It adds no security mechanism of its own.
sections.eli5: The new notice board is no easier or harder to tamper with than the old ones, so nothing new needs guarding.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned the Node Attribute TLV type value 5 from the range 3-32767 in the top level types in TE LSAs registry, as set out in RFC 3630. IANA also created a registry for the sub-TLVs of the Node Attribute TLV, with value 1 for the Node IPv4 Local Address sub-TLV and value 2 for the Node IPv6 Local Address sub-TLV.

Types 3-32767 are assigned by Standards Action. Types 32768-32777 are for experimental use, will not be registered with IANA and MUST NOT be mentioned by RFCs. Types 32778-65535 are not to be assigned at this time, and any assignment first requires a Standards Track RFC that covers the range in its IANA Considerations.
sections.eli5: A central librarian wrote down the numbers for the new notice types so everyone uses the same ones, and kept some numbers free for the future.

items.label: Node Attribute TLV
items.desc: Top-level TE LSA TLV carrying attributes of a router.

items.label: Node IPv4 Local Address sub-TLV
items.desc: One or more local IPv4 addresses as prefix length plus prefix.

items.label: Node IPv6 Local Address sub-TLV
items.desc: One or more local IPv6 addresses as prefix length, options and prefix.
